report.headline: Strong seeing-led engagement peaks in the middle; the product end-card lands below typical
report.summary: This CeraVe ad opens well above typical viewing and climbs quickly, driven almost entirely by seeing — faces and bodies carry the response throughout. Hearing contributes a clear boost in the opening seconds as Michael Cera introduces himself, but fades to near-zero by mid-video. Understanding stays modest all the way through. The peak runs from roughly seconds 8 to 14, where the spa parody and rock-climbing visuals combine with high face and body responses to produce the strongest engagement in the video. The second half gradually softens as the boardroom scene reduces visual intensity. The final product card with on-screen text and no people is the weakest stretch and dips below typical — an expected end-card drop but one worth noting because it arrives before the very last second.

moments.what_happens: Michael Cera speaks directly to camera, holds up the CeraVe jar, introduces himself and the product.
moments.brain_response: Opens above typical and rises steadily. Hearing is the strongest signal early, boosted by the opening speech. Seeing builds as the face and body become more prominent.
moments.suggestion: The opening is strong. The direct-to-camera address with the jar held up works well — keep the face large and the speech crisp in any re-edit.

moments.what_happens: Cut to close-up hands on skin, then a wide spa tent shot with Cera giving a massage, then two faces peering up from a massage table, then a rock climber scaling a cliff face.
moments.brain_response: The video's peak engagement. Seeing reaches its highest values (bodies above 0.8, faces above 0.5), well above typical. Hearing has faded but the pictures alone sustain the response. Overall is at its strongest here.
moments.suggestion: The absurdist spa-to-rock-climbing sequence is the most engaging passage. If you extend or tighten this ad, protect this stretch — the physical, body-forward imagery is doing the most work.

moments.what_happens: Three men pose together holding CeraVe jars in a fashion-shoot style.
moments.brain_response: Seeing remains clearly above typical (faces around 0.45, bodies around 0.4), but is declining from the peak. Overall holds above typical. Understanding edges up slightly as speech continues.
moments.suggestion: The trio shot sustains good engagement. The product is visible and the faces are prominent — no change needed, though cutting it shorter would lose little.

moments.what_happens: Boardroom scene: a crowd watches a presentation screen showing the earlier footage, with 'CeraVe Offices / Dermatologist Review' text on screen.
moments.brain_response: A gradual softening. Seeing (faces, bodies) continues to decline. Hearing drops to near zero or below. Understanding is the relatively strongest signal here, though still modest. Overall is the weakest passage before the end card.
moments.suggestion: The wide boardroom shot reduces face size and body prominence, which softens engagement. Cutting to a closer reaction shot of the dermatologists watching the screen could help maintain seeing through this reveal.

moments.what_happens: Product card: CeraVe jar on a table beside on-screen text reading 'Developed with dermatologists. Not Michael Cera.'
moments.brain_response: Seeing drops sharply below typical; hearing and understanding near zero. Overall falls to just below typical — the lowest stretch of the video outside the final second.
moments.suggestion: The punchline lands in text rather than on a face, which costs engagement. Keeping Michael Cera briefly in frame alongside the text — even as a small inset — before cutting fully to the product could soften the drop without losing the joke.

moments.what_happens: Final frame of the product card.
moments.brain_response: Overall drops sharply below typical. All seeing signals fall steeply. This is the lowest point in the video.

strengths: Seeing dominates from the first second and stays well above typical through the middle of the video, driven by strong face and body signals.
The opening — Michael Cera addressing camera and holding up the jar — builds quickly and combines hearing and seeing effectively.
The spa parody and rock-climbing sequence (seconds 7–14) is the peak of the video, with the highest body and face responses, showing the absurdist visual comedy is working hard.
The three-person fashion pose with product visible (seconds 16–18) sustains above-typical seeing even as the video winds down.
improvements: The boardroom scene (seconds 19–23) is the weakest passage before the end card; wider shots reduce face size and body presence, softening engagement at a key narrative moment.
Hearing fades to near zero or below from around second 19 onward — the back half of the ad is carried almost entirely by pictures, and a stronger audio element could support the final reveal.
Understanding remains modest throughout; the spoken punchline and on-screen text could be made more prominent or delivered face-to-camera to lift the social and speech response during the payoff.

The product card (seconds 27–29) drops below typical as soon as people leave the frame; even a brief return to a face alongside the product text would ease the dip at the moment the brand message lands.

report.headline: Strong, picture-led engagement throughout — seeing and hearing both carry this ad well above typical
report.summary: This CeraVe ad performs solidly above 0 for most of its 77 seconds, with seeing leading from around second 7 onward and hearing adding a strong second layer during the dialogue-heavy middle section. Understanding contributes positively too, particularly when speech is most active between seconds 10 and 22. The opening four seconds start below 0 — curtains with no face visible — but the response climbs quickly once a figure and then Michael Cera's face appear, reaching typical levels by second 5 and above typical by second 8. The strongest stretch runs from roughly seconds 10 to 30, where all three groups are above 0 together. The section from seconds 32 to 50 is the weakest part of the video: seeing holds up but hearing and understanding dip, and overall softens — an opportunity to add a stronger audio or speech element. The final logo card from second 74 onward produces the expected drop and is not a concern.

moments.what_happens: Dark curtains part; a silhouetted figure is barely visible. No face is shown clearly.
moments.brain_response: All groups start below 0. Seeing, hearing and understanding are all in negative territory, making this the lowest point of the video.
moments.suggestion: The opening could be pulled forward — showing Michael Cera's face or the product jar even a second or two earlier would help the response reach 0 faster.

moments.what_happens: Michael Cera steps into full light, faces camera, and holds up the CeraVe jar while speaking directly to the viewer. Hearing peaks around second 10 at its highest level in the video.
moments.brain_response: This is the strongest stretch overall. Seeing is well above 0, hearing reaches its peak, and understanding climbs above 0 for the first time. All three groups are positive together.

moments.what_happens: Cut to a spa scene: a man receiving a back massage in a white tent, with the CeraVe jar on a nearby stand. Michael Cera then appears as the masseur. Hearing and speech drop toward or below 0.
moments.brain_response: Seeing stays clearly above 0, driven by faces and bodies, but hearing falls to near 0 and understanding weakens. Overall softens compared to the previous peak. Pictures carry the moment; sound does not add much.
moments.suggestion: Adding a voiceover or keeping dialogue audible during this sequence would let hearing and understanding support the strong visual response rather than leaving it to carry the scene alone.

moments.what_happens: A surreal sequence: a group of men in white coats surrounds Cera, followed by a glowing curtain shot with the word SKIN on screen, then a lush fantasy garden and a CGI narwhal.
moments.brain_response: Seeing holds above 0, but hearing drops below 0 and understanding goes negative. This is the weakest stretch for hearing and understanding in the video, and overall is at its softest outside the opening.
moments.suggestion: This is the clearest opportunity in the ad. The visuals are inventive but the audio drops away. Even a brief line of dialogue or a stronger music cue here would lift hearing and understanding back above 0.

moments.what_happens: A split-screen of three different versions of the face, then Cera in a garden, then two men facing each other.
moments.brain_response: Hearing recovers to above 0, understanding edges positive, and overall stabilises. The picture carries more than the sound here — overall and the silent prediction are fairly close.

moments.what_happens: Cera stands flanked by two men in open lab coats, all holding CeraVe jars, staring into camera.
moments.brain_response: Seeing is above 0, hearing and understanding are close to 0 but positive. Overall is modest but above 0 — a stable close before the final curtain shot.

strengths: Seeing is above 0 for almost the entire video once Michael Cera's face appears at second 7, and faces and bodies stay strongly positive through to second 70.
The speech-heavy section from seconds 10 to 22 is the single strongest moment: hearing peaks at its highest level and understanding is clearly positive, giving all three groups a rare joint peak.
The product jar appears on screen alongside the face throughout most of the ad, keeping the brand visible during the highest-engagement stretches.
The overall level stays above 0 from second 8 to second 72, a long run of above-typical brain engagement relative to the model's baseline.
improvements: The first four seconds open below 0 across all groups. Moving a recognisable face or the product into the very first shot would close that gap faster.

Hearing and understanding both drop below or near 0 between seconds 44 and 51 — the narwhal and fantasy garden sequence — leaving seeing to carry the video alone. A voiceover or audible dialogue would strengthen this section.
Understanding stays negative for the first 11 seconds and dips again from seconds 32 to 36 and 46 to 50. Earlier and more sustained speech would keep this group contributing alongside seeing.

The spa and rock-climbing sequences from seconds 27 to 41 are visually strong but hearing is near 0 for much of that stretch. A music lift or spoken line during those cuts would better match the visual energy.

report.headline: B opens stronger and peaks higher in seeing; A sustains more over its longer second half
report.summary: These are two cuts of the same CeraVe campaign. B starts immediately with a face and speech, driving seeing and hearing above typical from second 0, and reaches its highest seeing response (faces +0.55, bodies +0.86) during the spa and comedy beats at 8–14 s. A spends its first 7 seconds on curtains and a product shot before engagement builds. Where they share material, B's tighter edit keeps seeing higher throughout; A's extended second half adds unique scenes that sustain a moderate response B never reaches.

differences.what_differs: A opens on dark curtains with no face for several seconds before cutting to the product jar and a hand; B cuts immediately to a face delivering speech. By A 6 s, faces are only +0.13 and overall is only +0.09, while B already has faces at +0.19 and overall at +0.14 with hearing above +0.28 from frame one.
differences.brain_response: B's immediate face-plus-speech opening engages seeing and hearing from the first second, whereas A's curtain-and-product cold open keeps all signals below typical for the first four seconds, a real gap in early engagement.

differences.what_differs: Both cuts share the spa massage scene, the massage-table comedy moment, and the rock-climbing sequence, but in A these run from about 27 s to 51 s while in B they are compressed into 7–15 s. In B, bodies peak at +0.86 and seeing at +0.50 during this block; in A the same material yields bodies peaking at +0.63 and seeing at +0.31.
differences.brain_response: B's earlier and faster presentation of the shared action and comedy material produces a markedly stronger seeing response, roughly double the body-area signal, suggesting the punchier pacing raises engagement above what A achieves with the same shots.

differences.what_differs: A contains an extended sequence unique to this cut: a mirror-room scene with multiple figures, a fantasy jungle environment with a narwhal, a split-screen of three faces, and a closing trio tableau with dermatologist-styled companions, running from roughly 44 s to 72 s. B has no equivalent material.
differences.brain_response: This stretch keeps A's overall response consistently above 0 (ranging from about +0.04 to +0.17) and seeing above 0 throughout, giving A a prolonged moderate engagement that B, ending at 30 s, never needs to sustain — an advantage in total coverage of the brand story even if individual peaks are lower than B's.

a_does_better: A's longer runtime lets it develop the brand narrative through more varied scenes — fantasy jungle, split-screen faces, and the extended dermatologist trio — keeping seeing and understanding signals above typical for nearly a minute.
The hearing signal in A rises to +0.50 around 10 s and stays elevated through the spoken comedy lines, matching or exceeding B's hearing level during shared material.
b_does_better: B's immediate face-and-speech opening means all three groups — seeing, hearing, and understanding — are above typical from the very first second, while A takes roughly 7 seconds to reach that point.

B achieves its peak seeing response (bodies +0.86, overall +0.25) during the shared spa and comedy material, roughly double A's seeing level at the equivalent moment, suggesting the compressed pacing is more arresting for that sequence.
suggestions: Consider moving A's opening so a face and the product appear within the first two seconds, matching B's cold-open structure, to close the early engagement gap before the curtain reveal pays off.

The fantasy jungle and narwhal sequence in A (around 48–55 s) shows seeing well above 0 but hearing dips below typical; adding music or a brief spoken line there could lift the overall response closer to the levels achieved during the earlier speech-driven stretch.
